news_drafts.headline: Cambridgeshire's schools deficit reached £96.3m at March 2026; £63.3m more forecast for 2026-27
news_drafts.lead:
Cambridgeshire County Council's cumulative deficit on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, rose from £62.851m to £96.3m over 2025-26, after an in-year deficit of £33.406m. The council's external auditor, KPMG, reports in its interim annual report that the increase came mainly from high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities, and grew broadly in line with the council's budgeted position.

The council estimates the government's new High Needs Stability Grant could provide about £88.3m, leaving an estimated £8.0m of the historic deficit to be met locally. The grant replaces the Safety Valve programme from 1 April 2026 and covers up to 90% of the cumulative deficit at 31 March 2026, subject to an approved Local SEND Reform Plan. The statutory override, a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet, has been extended to the end of 2027-28. The council's June 2026 SEND Reform data submission forecast an in-year deficit of £63.3m for 2026-27, against £33.4m in 2025-26. The grant was due to be confirmed in October 2026; the papers do not record the outcome. The council's risk register records £7.5m held in reserves.

KPMG retains one weakness from the prior year: a continuing significant weakness in value-for-money arrangements for governance of the schools grant. It says governance and monitoring strengthened during 2025-26 but had not yet shown that high needs pressures were under sustainable control at 31 March 2026.

news_drafts.headline: Cambridgeshire Pension Fund: KPMG sets £49m materiality for its 2025-26 audit
news_drafts.lead:
Cambridgeshire Pension Fund's external auditor, the accountancy firm KPMG, has set materiality for its audit of the fund's 2025-26 accounts at £49m. Materiality is the size of error that an auditor treats as large enough to matter to a reader of the accounts. The Pension Fund Board noted the audit plan at its meeting on 3 July 2026, and the minutes record: "Materiality had been set at £49 million."

KPMG calculated the figure as 1% of the fund's total draft assets as at 31 March 2025. Its plan lists two significant risks: management override of controls, and the valuation of level three assets, which are investments with no quoted market price.

According to the minutes, officers do not expect material differences on the fund's private equity investments.

news_drafts.headline: Cambridgeshire schools funding: historic commitments fall from £1.21m to £968k for 2027/28
news_drafts.lead:
Papers for Cambridgeshire's Schools Forum show the council's historic commitments falling from £1.21m in 2026/27 to an estimate of £968k in 2027/28. They sit within the dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools. The schools funding update for the forum's meeting on 6 November describes the change as a further 20% reduction.

The paper says the planned underspend on historic commitments is to "contribute towards DSG deficit recovery". A DSG deficit is an overspend on that grant, usually on support for children with special educational needs.

The commitments are part of the grant's central school services block, which the table puts at £5.341m in 2026/27 and £5.099m in 2027/28. The paper also says that funding for historic commitments that have now ended will be taken as a direct saving.

findings.headline: £1.6m of ASC debt is with Debt Collection Agencies or Legal, a decrease of £179k (10%) on this time last year
findings.detail: The paper says the legal cases are monitored between the council's Debt Team and Pathfinder Legal Services. Deceased-debt balances rose by £109k (1%) and are described as particularly complex to resolve.
findings.matters: Movement in the balance sent to external collection agencies or legal action shows whether escalation is reducing, which affects both recovery cost and write-off risk.
findings.figures: £1.6m with DCAs or Legal; £179k decrease (10%); deceased debt up £109k (1%); 11 accounts totalling £395k with pending property sale
findings.quote: £1.6m is currently either with Debt Collection Agencies or with Legal, a decrease of £179k (10%) from this time last year.

findings.headline: Additional Debt Officer resource started in June 2026, and a new Debt Team Manager started in September 2026
findings.detail: The paper lists these as completed actions under the restructure of the Debt Team, to increase recovery activity and provide stronger management support.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council would be interested in the staffing change made to recovery capacity, as it is one of the levers used to address the same aged-debt trend.
findings.figures: Additional Debt Officer resource from June 2026; new Manager from September 2026
findings.quote: Additional Debt Officer resource commenced in June 2026, to increase volume of resource on active recovery.

findings.headline: Customers with debt over 365 days fell to 825 from 868, while customers with overdue debt rose by 152 (7%) to 2,115
findings.detail: The paper compares the figures with the previous Audit Committee report. It says the reduction in long-running debtors is occurring alongside a rise in the total number of customers with overdue balances.
findings.matters: The split between total overdue customers and long-running customers shows whether the aged-debt problem is spreading or concentrating, which is useful for peer benchmarking.
findings.figures: 2,115 customers with overdue debt (up 152, 7%); 825 customers with debt over 365 days (down 43, 5%)
findings.quote: The volume of customers with debt over 365 days is 825, compared to 868 reported in the previous Audit Committee report, which a reduction of 43 (5%).

findings.headline: Place and Sustainability overdue debt fell 11% on the month to £7,426,430, but is 324% above last year's £2,976,408
findings.detail: The paper reports the monthly fall alongside the year-on-year rise. Its earlier text attributes the year-on-year increase in debt to Place and Sustainability partly to debt with other public bodies.
findings.matters: A large year-on-year rise in one directorate's overdue balance is a signal that a finance director or lender would want the cause of, especially where the debt is owed by public bodies.
findings.figures: £7,426,430 current; £8,325,968 previous month (-11%); £2,976,408 last year (324% increase); £3.67m year-on-year increase

findings.headline: Overdue NHS debt rose to £6,086,277, up 43% on the previous month and 145% on last year
findings.detail: NHS Services is the one directorate in the table where the paper's monthly and yearly trend columns both show a large increase, and the paper's own text describes the NHS-related figures as part of the debt owed by other public bodies.
findings.matters: Debt owed by other public bodies is typically low-risk for write-off but can carry long collection timelines, which a finance officer would need to plan cash flow around.
findings.figures: £6,086,277 (current month); £4,260,333 (previous month); £2,484,487 (last year); 43% month on month; 145% year on year

daily_post.headline: The Fund is overweight to alternatives, slightly overweight to listed equity and underweight to bonds relative to its benchmark allocation.
daily_post.lead: A finance director would want to know where the fund sits against its strategic allocation, and the paper's own traffic-light key treats an actual-allocation probability below 65% as a point to watch.
